passage:
"We won!" Nilesh burst through the door, bat on his shoulder. "Thirty-two runs, didi! I hit the ball so perfectly, nobody could stop me."
"Nice!" said Gurleen, looking up from her homework. "And last Sunday?"
"Last Sunday doesn't count. The umpire was Pinku's cousin. Totally unfair."
"You were bowled first ball."
"Because the bat was cracked! Anyone would get out with that bat."
"Isn't that the same bat?"
Nilesh looked at the bat. "It's different today."
"How?"
"Today I was playing properly."
Gurleen grinned. "So when you win, it's you. When you lose, it's the umpire and the bat?"
"Obviously," said Nilesh, and went off to find a snack.

qa.q: How many runs did Nilesh score today?
qa.a: Nilesh scored thirty-two runs.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh insist last Sunday doesn't count?
qa.a: Nilesh feels embarrassed about being bowled first ball, so blaming the umpire and the cracked bat lets him keep feeling like a great player.

qa.q: What question could help Nilesh learn from last Sunday?
qa.a: Someone could ask, 'If the bat and umpire were fine, what would you practise?' so he looks at his own play too.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Nilesh's two stories?
qa.a: Gurleen notices it's the same bat both days and finds it funny that wins belong to him and losses to someone else. 😅

grounding: A boy credits his skill for a win but blames the umpire and his bat for a loss.

passage: I'm Jatin, and last week I played two carrom matches at our society's summer games. In the first one I beat Ramesh from C-wing. I think I only blamed them because losing to a Class 3 girl made my face hot.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's little sister feel hearing she just got lucky?

passage:
Coach's notes, Under-11 football, Saturday
Yusuf scored twice in the first half and ran to the sideline shouting, "Told you I'm the best striker!" In the second half we conceded three and lost. Yusuf said the referee was blind, the ball was flat and the goalkeeper was "useless." He kicked his water bottle.
After the match I asked him to list two reasons we won the first half. He said, "Me and... me." I laughed and asked who passed to him both times. He thought and said, "Shreyas." Then I asked for one thing he could have done better in the second half. That took longer. Eventually: "I stopped running back."
Plan: next week, each player names one thing a teammate did well.
Coach Reena

qa.q: How many goals did Yusuf score in the first half?
qa.a: Yusuf scored twice in the first half.

qa.q: Why was it easier for Yusuf to blame the referee and the ball?
qa.a: Losing stung his pride, and blaming the referee and the flat ball protected his feeling of being the best striker.

qa.q: How did Coach Reena help Yusuf see his own part?
qa.a: Coach Reena asked who passed to him and what he could have done better, so Yusuf named Shreyas and 'I stopped running back' himself.

qa.q: How might the goalkeeper feel about being called useless?
qa.a: The goalkeeper probably felt blamed and hurt for a loss the whole team shared. 😔

grounding: A coach notes a boy crediting himself for goals but blaming the referee, ball and keeper for the loss.

passage:
Saturday
Today we had the badminton match in our building's parking lot. I played two games.
First game I played with Vinita didi's friend from B-block. I won 15 to 9! That is because I have a very strong smash. Didi said I am getting good. I am the best smasher in our wing.
Second game I played Vinita didi herself and I lost 6 to 15. But that was not fair. The shuttle was old and all the feathers were bent, so it went sideways every time. Also the wind came right when I hit. And the net was too high on my side.
Didi said, "Same shuttle, same net, same wind in the first game, na?" I said it was different. Then she told Ammi, "Your son is a sore loser."
Tomorrow I will bring a new shuttle.
Rafiq

qa.a: She could ask what he might practise to beat her next time, so Rafiq starts looking at his own play and not only the shuttle.

qa.q: How might Vinita didi see Rafiq's explanation of the second game?
qa.a: She probably finds it a bit funny and a bit frustrating, since she knows the shuttle, net and wind were the same in the first game he won.

passage:
At the Sunday fair in their village near Dharwad, children played marbles in the dusty ground behind the sweet stalls. Gautam, ten, won the first round against Jaya and scooped up all her marbles.
"Did you see that?" he told his friends. "Perfect aim. I've got the best thumb in the whole village."
In the second round Jaya knocked three of his marbles out of the ring and won them all back.
Gautam kicked the dust. "The ground is bumpy on my side. And that bullock cart shook everything when I was aiming. And your marbles are heavier."
Jaya held one up. "We swapped marbles after the first round, remember?"
"It was still the ground," Gautam said, turning away. But he picked a smooth spot for the third round, crouched lower, and kept glancing back at how Jaya held her thumb.

qa.q: What did Gautam say about his thumb after winning the first round?
qa.a: He said, "I've got the best thumb in the whole village."

qa.q: Why might blaming the ground and the cart feel easier for Gautam than admitting Jaya played better?
qa.a: Owning the win made him feel proud, and blaming things outside protects that proud feeling after he lost, so he does not have to feel less skilled.

qa.q: What small sign suggests Gautam might learn something despite blaming the ground?
qa.a: He crouched lower and kept glancing at how Jaya held her thumb, which shows a quiet chance to learn from her if he keeps watching.

qa.q: How might Jaya see Gautam's excuses?
qa.a: Jaya probably finds them unfair, and a bit amusing, since they had even swapped marbles, and she likely knows she simply played a better round.

grounding: It shows a boy crediting a marbles win to his skill and blaming his loss on the ground, a cart and the marbles.

passage: The colony match was cut to five overs because dark clouds were rolling in, and Varun's team had to bat fast. He hit two fours and a six, and they won with one ball left before the rain came down. "Did you see my shots?" he said to his sister Aparna, dripping on the doormat. "Pure talent. I read the bowler perfectly." Next Sunday, same five overs, same clouds. Varun was out first ball, bowled. "The bat's handle is loose," he announced, "and the umpire moved when the bowler ran in. Distracting." Aparna, who had watched from the balcony both times, handed him a towel. "Last week the bat was fine and the umpire was great?" Varun opened his mouth, then took the towel without answering.

qa.q: How many overs was the colony match cut to?
qa.a: Five overs.

qa.q: Why did Varun blame the bat and the umpire the second Sunday?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at being out first ball, so blaming the bat and umpire protected his pride, while the win had felt like pure talent.

qa.q: What could Varun ask himself after both matches?
qa.a: What part was his skill and what part was luck or conditions, asked the same way for the win and the loss.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Varun's two explanations?
qa.a: Aparna sees they don't match, noticing he credited himself for the win and blamed the bat and umpire for the loss.

grounding: A boy credits his own talent for a win and blames the bat and the umpire for a loss under the same conditions.

passage: On Sunday afternoon in their Jaipur flat, Mridul beat his sister Bhavna at ludo twice in a row. "I'm a genius at strategy," he announced, dancing round the sofa. "You have to plan every move." Bhavna rolled her eyes and set up the board again. In the third game, her tokens raced home while Mridul's stayed stuck at the start. He lost. "This dice is broken," he said, shaking it. "It only gives me ones." "Same dice as the first two games," said Bhavna. "Those were different. That was skill." Their grandfather looked up from his newspaper. "So the dice only breaks when you lose, Mridul?" Mridul folded his arms, glanced at the dice, then at Dadaji, and grinned a little sheepishly.

qa.q: How many times in a row did Mridul beat Bhavna?
qa.a: Twice in a row.

qa.q: Why did Mridul blame the dice in the third game?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and embarrassed at losing, so a broken dice was easier to believe than bad luck, while his wins had felt like genius.

qa.q: What could Mridul notice from Dadaji's question?
qa.a: That luck played a part in all three games, so the wins weren't only skill and the loss wasn't only the dice.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel hearing Mridul call his wins genius?
qa.a: Bhavna is probably amused and a bit annoyed, since the same dice decided every game.

grounding: A boy calls his board-game wins genius and blames the dice when he loses.

passage: My name is Pankaj, and this is about carrom with Ganga didi. Last summer, when I won, I always said, "See? I'm the best striker in the building." When I lost, it was different. "The board is tilted." "You distracted me." Once I threw the striker on the sofa, calling it unlucky. Ganga didi never argued. One evening she said, "Come here, chhote bhai," and wrote two lists on the back of a calendar: "Why Pankaj wins" and "Why Pankaj loses." Under wins, she wrote what I said: my skill. Under losses: board, striker, didi. She showed it to me without a word. It looked so silly I laughed. Then I felt a little ashamed. I still say "board is tilted" sometimes. But now I hear it.

passage:
Badminton coaching, under-11 group, Saturday. Coach's note.
Madhav won both his morning games against Avni and told the group, "That's my smash. Nobody can return it." In the afternoon he lost twice to her. First he said the shuttle was bent. Then that the net was higher on his side. Then that I had called a line wrong. I had. Once. He was also double-hitting and not moving his feet, which is why he lost.
After the session I asked him two questions: "What made you win this morning?" "My smash." "What made you lose this afternoon?" He began to list the shuttle and the net, then stopped, and said, "Maybe my feet." Next week I will ask every child both questions after every game, so it becomes a habit.

qa.q: What did Madhav blame first for his afternoon loss?
qa.a: He said the shuttle was bent.

qa.q: Why did Madhav say "Maybe my feet"?
qa.a: Once asked both questions side by side, he seemed to feel less defensive and could see he was blaming outside things for losses but crediting himself for wins.

qa.q: What is the coach's plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: To ask every child both questions after every game, so looking at their own part in wins and losses becomes a habit.

qa.q: How might Avni feel when Madhav blames the shuttle and the net?
qa.a: Avni might feel her win is being taken away from her, as if she didn't earn it.

grounding: A coach's note shows a boy crediting wins to his smash and blaming losses on the shuttle, the net and the umpire.

passage:
It was Makar Sankranti, and after the kites the village boys played cricket in the harvested field. Saurabh's team won the first match. "Because I'm the best batsman," he announced, puffing out his chest.

In the second match, he was out for zero. He threw down the bat. "This bat is cracked! And the bowler was throwing, not bowling!"

His sister Rajni, keeping score on a mud wall, called out, "It's the same bat you won with!"

"It cracked in between."

"And the same bowler?"

"He got better at cheating."

Rajni laughed. "So when you win, it's you. When you lose, it's the bat, the bowler and the field."

Saurabh scowled. But he picked up the bat and looked at it. There was no crack.

qa.q: Where did the boys play cricket?
qa.a: In the harvested field.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh blame the bat and bowler after losing?
qa.a: Saurabh felt embarrassed and frustrated, and blaming the bat and bowler protected his proud feeling of being the best.

qa.q: What did Rajni point out, and how could it help Saurabh?
qa.a: Rajni noticed he took credit for winning but blamed everything else for losing; seeing that could help him learn from both.

qa.q: How might the bowler feel being accused of cheating?
qa.a: The bowler might feel hurt and annoyed, since he was just bowling well.

grounding: During a harvest festival, a child credits his skill for winning but blames the bat and bowler for losing.

passage:
It was Chinese New Year in Singapore, and the cousins were playing badminton in the void deck. Wei beat Liam in the first game. "I'm just really good," he said.

In the second game, Liam won easily. Wei stamped his foot. "The wind was blowing my way. And my racket strings are loose."

"The wind was blowing both ways," said Liam. "And you used the same racket when you won."

"It got loose after."

"You always do this," Liam said. "When you win, you're good. When you lose, it's the wind."

Wei's grandmother said, "Wei, maybe both games were you. The good one and the bad one."

Wei frowned. He hadn't thought about it that way. If the losing was his too, then maybe he could get better.

qa.q: Where were the cousins playing badminton?
qa.a: In the void deck.

qa.q: Why did Wei blame the wind and racket after losing?
qa.a: Wei felt frustrated and embarrassed, and blaming the wind protected his feeling of being really good.

qa.q: What did Wei's grandmother say that helped?
qa.a: She suggested both games were Wei's, which let him see losing as something he could learn from.

qa.q: How might Liam feel when Wei blames the wind?
qa.a: Liam might feel annoyed that the win wasn't taken seriously.

grounding: During Chinese New Year, a child credits his skill for winning but blames the wind and racket for losing.

passage:
During Christmas week, the school chess club held a mini-tournament in the library. Nitin won his first game quickly. "I'm a natural," he told Gargi.

In the second game, he lost to a Class 4 boy. "It's too noisy in here," he grumbled. "And that boy took too long to move. It put me off."

Gargi, the club's student captain, raised an eyebrow. "It was just as noisy when you won."

"Well, I was lucky to focus then."

"So winning was you being a natural, and losing was the noise?"

Nitin crossed his arms. Then he looked at the board. He'd moved his queen without checking. Twice.

"Maybe I made a mistake," he mumbled.

"Want to see where?" Gargi asked. She set up the pieces again.

qa.q: Where did the chess club hold the mini-tournament?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: Why did Nitin blame the noise after losing?
qa.a: Nitin felt embarrassed and wanted to protect his proud feeling of being a natural, so blaming the noise felt easier.

qa.q: What did Gargi do that helped Nitin learn?
qa.a: Gargi pointed out the room was equally noisy both times, then offered to show him where he went wrong.

qa.q: How might the Class 4 boy feel hearing Nitin's excuse?
qa.a: The boy might feel his win wasn't respected, though he played fairly.

grounding: During Christmas week, a child credits his talent for a chess win but blames the noise and opponent for a loss.

passage:
Saturday, first week of the summer holidays: Tanvir's team won the gully match by six runs. "That's because I batted like a pro," he told Ira, twirling his bat. "Nobody can bowl to me."
Tuesday: Hot wind blew dust down the lane. Tanvir was out on the second ball, and his team lost. He threw the bat down. "The bat's cracked. And the umpire's blind. That was never out!" Ira, who had been umpiring, crossed her arms.
Friday: Ira drew a chalk line down the wall and wrote two columns, WINS and LOSSES. "So whose fault?" she asked. Tanvir looked at the wall, then at his dusty sandals. "Maybe I swing too early," he mumbled. "Sometimes." He picked up the same bat and asked her to bowl.

qa.q: By how many runs did Tanvir's team win on Saturday?
qa.a: By six runs.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir blame the bat and the umpire on Tuesday?
qa.a: Losing made him feel embarrassed and angry, and blaming the bat and the umpire protected his idea of himself as the best batter.

qa.q: What helped Tanvir look at his own part?
qa.a: Ira's two chalk columns, which made him look at wins and losses the same way and ask whose part each one was.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Tanvir calls the umpire blind?
qa.a: Ira, who was umpiring, likely feels annoyed and unfairly blamed for his loss.

grounding: Shows a child crediting his own skill for a win and blaming the umpire and the bat for a loss.
